name: Swatow (Shantou) typhoon (1922)
when: 27 July–3 August 1922; landfall night of 2–3 August
headline: A strong typhoon with a central pressure of 932 hPa or lower drove a surge of at least 3.7 m into Shantou and the surrounding coast at night.
numbers: 27 July–3 August 1922; landfall night of 2–3 August
≈5,000 in the city (contemporary report) plus ≈50,000 in the surrounding area; above 60,000 per NOAA
Low: compilation figure without a traceable contemporary count
timeline: Landfall near Shantou; pressure 932 hPa or lower; surge at least 12 ft (3.7 m).

The weather setup: The storm crossed the Philippine Sea and northern Luzon and entered the South China Sea, then struck the Chinese coast near Shantou late on 2 August. The lowest recorded pressure was 932 hPa; the Japan Meteorological Agency's best track gives peak 10-minute winds of about 155 km/h. The surge rose at least 12 feet above normal at Shantou.
What made it so deadly: Shantou was a crowded treaty port of about 65,000 people on low land at the mouth of the Han River, surrounded by densely populated coastal plain. The surge and flooding hit at night.
The death toll and why it is uncertain: A contemporary report in Monthly Weather Review (Hurd, 1922) put deaths in the city at about 5,000. A later chronology (Selga) adds about 50,000 in the surrounding area and says the total may have exceeded 100,000; NOAA lists more than 60,000. The higher figures depend on estimates for the countryside, where there was no count.
